title: Pilot weekly velocity checkpoint - benchmark readout (BlueKite Diagnostics)
topics: KV cache and prefix reuse impact
header: Date: 2026-08-04 | Start: 14:00 UTC | Duration: 55m | Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Daniel Cho (Redwood SE), Priya Desai (Redwood CSM), Maya Singh (BlueKite Head of ML), Carlos Rodriguez (BlueKite Infra), Hannah Lee (BlueKite CTO), Omar Nader (BlueKite SRE)
summary: Week 2 POC readout focusing on latency/throughput vs the incumbent provider. Redwood presented aggregate bench CSV and routing experiments. Key findings: p50 close to incumbent, p95 shows 10-25% improvement in most configs but a tail regression on 8k sequences without KV warmup. Action: Daniel to run KV-warmup + 2x batching test, Ava to send consolidated cost delta, BlueKite to share real traffic shapes and enable dedicated slot for mid-week load test.
transcript:
[00:00:00] Ava Martinez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We wanted to walk through the week two bench and routing experiments we ran. Hi Maya, hi team.
[00:00:10] Maya Singh: Hi Ava, thanks—we're curious about the p95 numbers you flagged in the agenda. We saw the spreadsheet but had some questions.
[00:00:18] Daniel Cho: great, so I'll start with the headline. We ran three main profiles: short chat (<=256 tokens), medium (1k tokens), and long-form (8k window) with kv prefix caching enabled for the medium and long tests where applicable. The aggregated CSV is in the shared drive: https://redwood.app/bench/bluekite-aug4 (note: internal link).
[00:00:40] Carlos Rodriguez: quick question, the baseline provider—were they using quantized models or the same fp16 setup?
[00:00:46] Daniel Cho: Baseline used their usual A100 fp16 variants; we compared against our bfloat16 optimized runtime and also a 4-bit quantized run for cost deltas. For fairness we gave two configs: parity (fp16) and cost-optimized (4-bit).
[00:00:58] Hannah Lee: ok that helps. Show us numbers.
[00:01:02] Daniel Cho: p50 for short chat—Redwood 70ms, baseline 75ms, so roughly 7% faster. For medium 1k, p50 Redwood 210ms vs baseline 225ms. Throughput (concurrent RPS) at target latency SLO: Redwood handled 180 rps vs baseline 160 rps on the same reserved instance tier.
[00:01:26] Maya Singh: those look good, what about tails? p95/p99 are what matter to us.
[00:01:30] Daniel Cho: here's where it gets interesting. For medium, p95 Redwood is at 480ms vs baseline 530ms—about 9% better. p99s are within noise for medium. For 8k sequences, with cold-kv (no warmup), we saw a p95 regression in some runs: Redwood 1.9s vs baseline 1.6s. But when we ran with KV warmup (prefix reuse prepopulated), Redwood p95 dropped to 1.3s—so the KV cache behavior and our warmup policy materially changes the tail.
[00:02:07] Omar Nader: that's the key—our production workload has lots of long-context bursts with low prefix reuse initially, so cold-kv behavior matters.
[00:02:13] Priya Desai: to add, the 4-bit quantized runs shaved unit cost by ~38% but increased p95 by ~12% on long sequences, mostly due to extra kernel marshalling overhead.
[00:02:26] Carlos Rodriguez: can we see token-per-second throughput for the 8k tests? numbers please.
[00:02:30] Daniel Cho: sure—8k with warm KV: 220 tokens/sec sustained per GPU, without warm: 140 tokens/sec during tail spikes. Baseline quoted 180 tokens/sec steady but larger variance.
[00:02:45] Maya Singh: interesting, so Redwood beats baseline on steady-state but has a cold-start tail unless we seed caches. Would dedicated slots solve that?
[00:02:54] Ava Martinez: yes, dedicated capacity with pinned models and pinned KV strategy reduces variance. We can provision reserved slots so the KV is prewarmed and the model stays hot. That was part of the Dedicated pitch.
[00:03:06] Hannah Lee: what's the cost delta if we go dedicated for our expected 99th-percentile traffic?
[00:03:10] Ava Martinez: upfront reserved commitment increases fixed cost, but unit cost per token decreases. For your projected 10M tokens/day, the committed Dedicated plan reduced per-token cost by ~22% versus hosted quantized runs when we factor in throughput gains. I'll send a modelled sheet.
[00:03:25] Maya Singh: please do. Also, can you run a run with 2x batching on the long sequence to see if it smooths p95 without harming p50?
[00:03:32] Daniel Cho: yes, next run will be: KV warmup ON, batching factor 2, sequence 8k, quantized and fp16 variants. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec.
[00:03:41] Carlos Rodriguez: we can provide representative traffic shapes and sample payloads—that should make the lab tests more realistic. I'll drop them in the shared folder by EOD Tuesday.
[00:03:49] Omar Nader: one more operational note: our SREs need to see connection limits and TLS termination details—do you have docs?
[00:03:55] Priya Desai: yes, security appendix and network config are in the shared security pack. We'll include SAML/SSO notes and KMS integration steps in the follow-up.
[00:04:03] Maya Singh: on the regression for cold-kv—any quick mitigation during the pilot? Some kind of graceful fallback to baseline for the first N requests?
[00:04:11] Daniel Cho: we have routing policies—one approach is canary or staged fallback: route initial requests to the incumbent for new prefixes until KV hit rate improves, then switch to Redwood. Another is prefill the KV with recent prefixes from your traffic capture. We can demo both.
[00:04:25] Hannah Lee: would that require client changes?
[00:04:27] Ava Martinez: no client changes if you use our routing layer—it's policy driven. If you wanted an explicit client-side change we can provide a lightweight SDK toggle.
[00:04:36] Maya Singh: latency SLA—what can Redwood guarantee during the pilot?
[00:04:40] Ava Martinez: for hosted pilots we target p95 SLOs in the readme but no formal SLA; for Dedicated we can agree on contractual SLOs. For the pilot, we'll aim for p95 to be no worse than baseline in production-like run, otherwise we'll adjust routing.
[00:04:54] Carlos Rodriguez: ping on SOC2 docs and data residency—the decision buyer will ask.
[00:04:58] Priya Desai: sending SOC2 attestation and the data residency whitepaper in the follow-up. Also timeline for a short security review if you want to invite your InfoSec.
[00:05:08] Maya Singh: yes please, loop in InfoSec.
[00:05:11] Daniel Cho: back to benches—one anomaly we found: under bursty arrivals with mixed short/long sequences our batching heuristic occasionally increased head-of-line blocking; we adjusted the batching timeout and that reduced p95 by ~15%. We'll include that config in the runbook.
[00:05:24] Ava Martinez: action items we'll capture; quick recap: Daniel will run KV-warmup + 2x batch tests and post CSVs; Ava will send cost modelling and dedicated slot pricing; Carlos will upload traffic shapes; Priya will send SOC2/KMS docs; team to reconvene mid-week after the new runs.
[00:05:40] Maya Singh: sounds good. One last Q: are you able to run an end-to-end check with our sample prod payloads and our auth flow (SAML) for a dry run?
[00:05:48] Priya Desai: yes we can schedule a dry run—need your SSO contact to provision.
[00:05:52] Hannah Lee: Omar will share details.
[00:05:55] Ava Martinez: great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the links and dates.
[00:06:00] [meeting ends]
